chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding in what amount the thief's hand is cut off, so he said: 'In a quarter of a dinar.' I said to him, 'In two dirhams?' He said, 'In a quarter of a dinar, regardless of what value the dinar reaches.'
I said to him, 'Do you see one who steals less than a quarter of a dinar? Does the name 'thief' apply to him, and is he considered a thief with Allah in that state?'

He said: 'Whoever steals anything from a Muslim that has been secured and protected, the name 'thief' applies to him and he is a thief with Allah, but the hand is not cut off except in a quarter of a dinar or more.'
And if the hand of the thief were cut off for what is less than a quarter of a dinar, you would find most people with their hands cut off.

key_terms.حَوَاهُ وَأَحْرَزَهُ: Secured and protected (conditions for theft liability)
key_terms.رُبُعِ دِينَارٍ: Quarter of a dinar (minimum threshold for hadd punishment)
key_terms.يُقْطَعُ: To be cut off (referring to the hand)

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum value of gold required for cutting the hand of a thief in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the ontological status of being a 'thief' (sariq) in the sight of Allah, which applies to any secured item, and the jurisprudential application of hadd punishment, which requires a minimum value of a quarter dinar. This distinction reflects the Shia scholarly principle of separating moral culpability from legal penalty, ensuring that the severe punishment of amputation is reserved for significant thefts to avoid burdening the general populace with excessive penalties for minor infractions.
